---
title: "Rotary embeddings are just a rotation"
description: "RoPE looks like a trick until you write the inner product out. Then it is one line of linear algebra."
date: 2026-08-20
categories: [transformers, positional-encoding, notes]
image: thumbnail.png
bibliography: ../../references.bib

Rotary position embeddings [@su2024roformer] get described as "encoding absolute
position in a way that makes attention depend on relative position." That sentence
is true and it explains nothing. Here is the actual mechanism, which is one
rotation and one identity.

## The setup

Take a query vector $q \in \RR^{d}$ with $d$ even. Split it into $d/2$ consecutive
pairs of coordinates. Read each pair as a point in the plane.

Now pick a set of frequencies, one per pair:

$$
\theta_m = b^{-2m/d}, \qquad m = 0, 1, \dots, \tfrac{d}{2} - 1,
$$ {#eq-freqs}

with base $b = 10000$ in the original paper. Pair $0$ spins fast, pair $d/2 - 1$
spins slowly.

For a token at position $p \in \NN$, define the block-diagonal matrix

$$
R_p = \bigoplus_{m=0}^{d/2-1}
\begin{pmatrix}
\cos p\theta_m & -\sin p\theta_m \\
\sin p\theta_m & \phantom{-}\cos p\theta_m
\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-rot}

$R_p$ rotates pair $m$ by the angle $p\theta_m$. That is the whole construction.
Apply $R_p$ to the query at position $p$ and $R_s$ to the key at position $s$.

## Why relative position falls out

Each block of @eq-rot is a plane rotation, so $R_p$ is orthogonal and
$R_p^{-1} = R_p\T$. Rotations in a plane compose by adding angles, block by block,
which gives $R_p\T R_s = R_{s-p}$. The attention logit is then

$$
\inner{R_p q}{R_s k} = q\T R_p\T R_s\, k = q\T R_{s-p}\, k .
$$ {#eq-relative}

The left side is built from absolute positions. The right side depends only on
$s - p$. Nothing was approximated. The relative-position property is the
composition law for rotations, and that is all it is.

::: {.callout-note}
## Contrast with ALiBi
ALiBi [@press2022alibi] gets relative position by *adding* a term proportional to
$-\abs{s-p}$ to the logit. RoPE gets it by *rotating* the vectors, so the
positional signal lives in the geometry of $q$ and $k$ rather than in an additive
bias. One consequence: RoPE leaves the norms $\norm{q}$ and $\norm{k}$ untouched.
:::

## What the kernel looks like

The useful question is what @eq-relative does to a logit as distance grows. Fix
random $q$ and $k$, then sweep the offset $\Delta = s - p$.

::: {#cell-fig-rope-kernel .cell fig-height='4' fig-width='7' execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d, base = 64, 10_000.0

theta = base ** (-2 * np.arange(d // 2) / d)   # eq. 1

def logit(q, k, delta):
    """q^T R_delta k, pairwise, so it stays O(d)."""
    q0, q1 = q[0::2], q[1::2]
    k0, k1 = k[0::2], k[1::2]
    a = np.outer(delta, theta)                 # (n_delta, d/2)
    c, s = np.cos(a), np.sin(a)
    rot0 = k0 * c - k1 * s                     # rotate the key pairs
    rot1 = k0 * s + k1 * c
    return (q0 * rot0 + q1 * rot1).sum(axis=1)

delta = np.arange(0, 512)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for i in range(3):
    q = rng.normal(size=d) / np.sqrt(d)
    k = rng.normal(size=d) / np.sqrt(d)
    ax.plot(delta, logit(q, k, delta), lw=1.1,
            alpha=0.85, label=f"pair {i}")

ax.axhline(0, color="0.7", lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel(r"relative offset  $\Delta = s - p$")
ax.set_ylabel(r"logit  $q^\mathsf{T} R_\Delta k$")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Attention logit $q^\mathsf{T} R_\Delta k$ against relative offset, for three random query-key pairs at $d=64$. The signal does not decay monotonically. It oscillates, and the envelope is set by the slow frequencies.](index_files/figure-html/fig-rope-kernel-output-1.png){#fig-rope-kernel width=664 height=470}
:::
:::


@fig-rope-kernel is the part that surprised me the first time. There is no clean
distance decay. The logit wobbles, and whether a far-away token is boosted or
suppressed depends on where the phases happen to land. Long-context tricks that
change $b$ in @eq-freqs are all, in effect, stretching this curve sideways so the
phases the model trained on still line up.

## The one-liner

RoPE is: rotate each coordinate pair by an angle proportional to position, and
lean on $R_p\T R_s = R_{s-p}$. Everything else is choosing $\theta_m$.

::: {.column-margin}
Worth checking yourself: set $b = 1$ in the code above and every pair spins at the
same rate, which collapses the kernel to a single cosine.
:::
